subsystems.name: Unit cell (catom / module)
subsystems.role: the building block: a small robot that can attach to neighbours, then detach and crawl to a new position to reshape the whole object.
parts: on-board chip for logic and communication

subsystems.name: Actuation and latching
subsystems.role: moves each module relative to its neighbours one step at a time, and holds the assembled shape rigidly afterwards.

subsystems.name: Power and data distribution
subsystems.role: delivers energy and commands into a dense lattice without wiring every module individually.
parts: conductive bus running through the lattice contacts

subsystems.name: Control software
subsystems.role: converts a wanted shape into millions of safe, collision-free module moves.

subsystems.name: Sensing and user interface
subsystems.role: lets the surface know what the user needs and stop before hurting them.
parts: force and proximity sensors in the skin

subsystems.name: Deformable skin
subsystems.role: the visible, comfortable surface over the lattice.

buildSteps.title: Choose the unit size
buildSteps.detail: Small modules give finer shapes but weaker force and absurd part counts: a sofa-sized volume built from 1 mm cubes is on the order of a billion modules, against roughly ten million for 5 mm cubes.

buildSteps.title: Batch-fabricate the modules
buildSteps.detail: Micro-machining or MEMS-style wafer processes would produce electrostatic actuators, electrodes, latch faces and a small chip in one flow, then singulate them into individual units.

buildSteps.title: Give each module power and a voice
buildSteps.detail: Contacts on the faces pass both electricity and data so that a module is powered as soon as it docks; each carries enough stored energy to make its next move.

buildSteps.title: Write the distributed control
buildSteps.detail: A planner breaks a desired shape into module moves, and local rules let each module decide when to detach without deadlocking the lattice or dropping unloaded sections.

buildSteps.title: Assemble a lattice and scale it up
buildSteps.detail: Modules are packed into a self-supporting block; making enough of them cheaply, and getting yield high enough that faulty cells can be tolerated, is the manufacturing wall.

buildSteps.title: Apply the skin
buildSteps.detail: A stretchable sheet is bonded over the lattice so the object reads as a smooth surface rather than a stack of robots.

buildSteps.title: Add sensing and safety rules
buildSteps.detail: Force limits, jam detection and fail-safe rigid modes are programmed in so the furniture cannot crush a limb or collapse when power fails.

buildSteps.title: Commission for one room
buildSteps.detail: The unit learns its lattice layout, then is taught a small library of shapes — seat, bed, table — rather than free-form metamorphosis.

prerequisites.why: they have been built in planar arrays, but force falls steeply with size, so a module can move itself rather than lift a load — structural strength must come from the whole lattice.

prerequisites.tech: Micro-fabrication with on-board logic and power
prerequisites.why: MEMS devices with integrated circuits exist, but no free-moving particle yet combines actuator, chip, latch and energy storage in one cheap unit.

prerequisites.tech: Power and data delivery through a dense lattice
prerequisites.why: contact buses and inductive coupling work at small scale; distributing watts through millions of sliding contacts reliably is unsolved.
demonstrated in simulation and on small modular-robot chains of tens of units, not on millions of independent cells.
furniture-scale objects need billions of modules, so unit cost must fall far below anything micro-robotics achieves today.

pathway.milestone: tabletop shape displays and modular robots: pin-array surfaces that raise and lower rods, and centimetre-scale modules that dock into small structures such as a stool
pathway.unlocks: proof that reconfigurable matter is physically possible at small scale.

pathway.milestone: centimetre-scale modules in the thousands, with magnetic latching, forming metre-sized surfaces
pathway.unlocks: a bench or wall panel that genuinely changes shape, at high cost and low load.

pathway.milestone: specialist applications before furniture: reconfigurable jigs and tooling, adaptive seats for people who cannot reposition themselves, and inspection robots
pathway.unlocks: a market that pays for the technology while reliability improves.

pathway.milestone: a room-scale lattice of millimetre catoms under a stretchable skin, mimicking the claytronics concept pursued in early research programmes on programmable matter
pathway.unlocks: interiors that morph between furniture types on demand — only if power, cost, strength and safety are all solved together.
